9. FISHERIES
Introduction
9.1.1.1 This section presents the fisheries baseline conditions within the Assessment Area,
and the assessment results of the potential fisheries impacts resulting from the
construction and operation of the Project. The location plan and description of the
Project are presented in Figure 1.1 and Section 2, respectively.
9.1.1.2 According to the EIAO-TM and Appendix H of the EIA Study Brief (ESB-373/2025),
baseline conditions for fisheries resources were evaluated based on information
from available literature and site visits conducted for the purposes of this EIA.
Measures required to mitigate any identified adverse impacts are recommended,
where appropriate, and residual impacts are assessed.
Environmental Legislation, Standards and Guidelines
9.2.1.1 Reference was made to the following HKSAR Government ordinances, regulations,
standards, guidelines and documents when identifying, evaluating and assessing
potential impacts of the Project on the fisheries resources:
• The Environmental Impact Assessment Ordinance (Cap. 499);
• Annexes 9 and 17 of the EIAO-TM;
• EIAO Guidance Note No. 15/2023 - Methodologies for Fisheries Baseline
Surveys; and
• Water Pollution Control Ordinance (Cap. 358).
Assessment Methodology
Assessment Area
9.3.1.1 The Assessment Area includes areas within a 500 m distance from the proposed
San Tin section of the NMH alignment and associated works (i.e. the Project
Boundary) (Figure 9).
Methodology
9.3.2.1 Literature review and desktop study were conducted to collate the latest baseline
conditions regarding culture fisheries resources within the Assessment Area. A list
of available literature is provided in Table 9.1 below.

9.3.2.2 In addition to the literature review with recent aerial photographs, fisheries baseline
surveys in the form of site visits were also undertaken over a 9-month period, i.e.
between April 2025 and December 2025, in accordance with the EIA Study Brief
(ESB-373/2025) for the verification of the ponds and associated fisheries activities,
with particular focus on those within the Project Boundary, where accessible. The
conditions of the fishponds and the fisheries activities were observed and recorded.
Drone photos were taken to facilitate the assessment of inaccessible ponds within
the Assessment Area. Observation was made on the presence of any aquaculture
practice and activities (e.g. draining, liming, re-profiling, stocking, feeding and
harvesting), evidence of any recently used devices/equipment and sign of
vegetation management.
9.3.2.3 General activity status of the fishponds was categorised as follows:
• Active: Utilised for commercial aquaculture activities, including commercial
fishponds, fish fry ponds, and indoor fish farms;
• Inactive: No commercial aquaculture activities and management (e.g.
overgrown vegetation at pond bunds hindering culture activities, and lack of
equipment such as aerator). However, there should be no major physical
constraints to its resumption in the short-term. Examples include fishponds with
fish present in non-commercial quantities, and ponds for recreational fishing;
• Abandoned: Ponds with physical evidence that aquaculture has not been
practised for years (typically ponds with overgrown vegetation or dried up)
and/or obvious physical constraints to the resumption of fisheries activities (e.g.
inaccessible or fenced off); and

9.3.2.4 The status of fishpond management was investigated with reference made to the
evidence of aquaculture activities, such as the presence of aquaculture operation
(e.g. stocking, feeding, harvesting), management activities (e.g. pumping of water,
draining, dredging, re-profiling and maintenance grass trimming), and the presence
of any associated equipment (e.g. aerators, conditions of pond bund and fodder)
and their conditions. Attention was also given to any watercourses which potentially
serve as water sources for fishponds.
Fisheries Baseline Condition from Literature Review
Description of the Environment and Baseline Condition
Aquaculture (Pond Fish Culture) Activities and Resources
9.4.1.1 Fishponds were mainly identified at the southeast of Nam Sang Wai (NSW), west
of the existing San Tin Highway, and west of the Ngau Tam Mei Water Treatment
Works (NTMWTW). Some scattered fishponds were recorded at the northeast of
the San Tin Barracks, west of the Sheung Yue River (SYR), and Tit Hang. Pond
fish culture of various statuses was identified, including active, inactive and
abandoned fishponds (Figures 9.1 to 9.9 refer).
Other Fisheries Resources
9.4.1.2 No other fisheries resources such as capture fisheries or other aquaculture (e.g.
Fish Culture Zones or oyster culture) were recorded within the Assessment Area.
Considering the absence of these other fisheries resources, potential impacts on
these resources were not anticipated. Therefore, no further detailed assessment
was required in these other fisheries resources (Figures 9.1 to 9.9 refer).
Pond Culture Fisheries Activities and Resources
Desktop Study
9.4.2.1 Pond fish culture in Hong Kong has been centred in the northwest New Territories.
About 88% of the fish farms are engaged in polyculture (including bighead carp,
grass carp, common carp and silver carp in combination with tilapia or grey mullet).
The remaining 12% practise monoculture of carnivorous species such as giant
groupers, seabreams and spotted scat in brackish fishponds near the coastline
(AFCD, 2026).
9.4.2.2 According to the data from AFCD on aquaculture in Hong Kong, the production of
pond fish was stabilised until 2021 but has declined significantly since 2022. Annual
pond fish production and fishpond areas in the territory are listed in Table 9.2 below.
Local pond fish production only accounted for about 3.9% of total consumption of
freshwater fish in 2024 (AFCD, 2025).

Fisheries Baseline Condition from Recent Survey
Recent Site Visit Findings
9.5.1.1 The distribution and physical conditions of the fishponds are largely similar and
comparable to the baseline conditions identified from literature review, which are
considered relevant for the assessment. Based on observations from site visits,
fishponds (including active, inactive and abandoned fishponds) and other non-
fisheries related ponds were recorded across the Assessment Area, numbered as
P#1 – P#258 (Figures 9.1 to 9.9 refer).
9.5.1.2 Among the fishponds recorded within the Project Boundary, majority of the
fishponds were active fishponds. Active fishponds identified within the Project
Boundary were concentrated to the west of NTMWTW and some scattered ones
west of SYR. Direct rainfall was the major water source of fishponds within the
Assessment Area. Other potential water sources for fishponds include wells and
from adjacent fishponds where water was pumped and drained from one pond to
another.
9.5.1.3 Apart from fishponds, ten ponds were identified as “Other Ponds (non-fisheries
related)”, including P#48 and P#49 (non-fisheries related ponds within Park Yoho
and Sha Po Marsh area, Figure 9.2), P#58, P#61-#64 (Yuen Long Bypass
Floodway Engineered Wetland, Figure 9.2), P#84 and P#85 (Pok Wai Floodwater
Pumping Station, Figure 9.3), and P#247 (i.e. Kwu Tung Reservoir, Figure 9.8).
Except P#247, all of these “Other Ponds (non-fisheries related)” were recorded
outside the Project Boundary.
9.5.1.4 A total of 258 ponds were identified within the Assessment Area. Among these
ponds, 34 ponds (including 28 active fishponds, four inactive fishponds, one
abandoned fishpond, one “other pond”) fall wholly or partially within the Project
Boundary. Among the 28 active fishponds, five of them are excluded from land
resumption and no direct impact is expected to these fishponds. The active
fishponds accounts for 36.3% in terms of pond areas within Assessment Area, and
44.2% within the Project Boundary (Table 9.3).

P#159) was within the site areas of concurrent project in NTM area (i.e.
Development at Ngau Tam Mei Area) where the fishpond is expected to be lost
under the concurrent project..
9.5.2.5 These inactive fishponds were observed with no current utilisation for commercial
aquaculture activities and lack of management for pond fish culture, but the pond
structure remained relatively intact, with potential to be resumed for fisheries
production with maintenance and management.
Abandoned Ponds
9.5.2.6 Abandoned fishponds were also recorded across the Assessment Area, including
those along KTMDC (i.e. P#1, P#5-16, P#21-25, P#43 and P#45-47), to the
southeast of NSW (i.e. P#54 and P#66), west of San Tin Highway (i.e. P#77-78,

P#202 and P#204) and northeast of San Tin Barracks (i.e. P#214-215, P#221-226,
P#228, P#230-231, P#245 and P#258) (Figure 9.4 refers). Except P#185 which fall
within the Project Boundary identified at the west of the NTMWTW, other
abandoned ponds were located outside the Project Boundary. Two abandoned
fishponds were within the site areas of concurrent project in NTM area (i.e. P#144-
145) where the fishponds are expected to be lost under the concurrent project.
9.5.2.7 All of these abandoned fishponds were observed with no current utilisation for
commercial aquaculture activities and with overgrown vegetation. The abandoned
and overgrown structure of these fishponds would be a physical constraint to the
resumption of fisheries activities in a short period of time.

Construction Phase – Direct Impact

wetland compensation area after the completion of construction works as an
ecological enhancement measure of the overall NMH Project as detailed under
Section 8.11 of this report. Key fisheries activities, resources and production within
the Project Boundary, including active fishponds and inactive fishponds, were

Loss of Active Fishponds
9.6.2.2 Within the Project Boundary, active fishponds under active production were mainly
located in NTM area. A total of 25 active fishponds were identified in NTM area and
three were located in Ki Lun Tsuen area (Figure 9.4 and Figure 9.6 refer). To
minimise the direct impact to active fishponds, five fishponds (i.e. P#170-173 and
P#244) are excluded from land resumption and no direct impact is expected. Quite
a number of active fishponds in NTM area were utilised for cultivation of non-edible
ornamental fish, such as Koi, while some were found to be utilised for cultivation of
edible fish species.
9.6.2.3 Direct loss of fisheries production, resources and aquaculture activities at active
fishponds (about 1.5 ha) (i.e. 23 fishponds) would be resulted from the Project
(Table 9.5 refers). The expected direct loss account for about 62.5% of the total
fishpond areas within the Project Boundary. The expected direct loss also accounts
for 0.1% of fishpond areas in Hong Kong in terms of aquaculture. Considering the
area of direct loss of active fishponds does not account for a significant proportion
of the total fishpond areas in Hong Kong and quite a number of active fishponds
were utilised for cultivation of non-edible ornamental fish, the impact on fisheries
resources and potential contribution to the annual fisheries production in Hong
Kong is considered to be low.

9.6.2.4 For inactive fishponds, the Project would result in direct loss of 0.2 ha fishponds (i.e.
four fishponds) in NTM area (Figure 9.4 and Table 9.5 refer). The expected direct
loss of inactive fishponds accounts for about 8.3% of the total fishpond areas within
the Project Boundary. In terms of fishpond areas in Hong Kong, the expected direct
loss of inactive fishponds would account for <0.1%.
9.6.2.5 These inactive fishponds were observed without aquaculture activities during recent
site visits. Given the small loss of inactive fishponds which does not account for a
significant proportion of the total fishponds area in Hong Kong and no evidence of
commercial aquaculture activities was observed in these inactive fishponds during
recent observation, the impact on fisheries resources and fisheries production is
considered very low.
Loss of Abandoned Fishponds
9.6.2.6 For abandoned fishponds, the Project would result in direct loss of 0.7 ha fishponds
(i.e. one fishpond) in NTM area (Figure 9.4 and Table 9.5 refer). The expected
direct loss of abandoned fishponds would be about 29.2% of the total fishpond
areas within the Project Boundary. In terms of fishpond areas in Hong Kong, the
expected direct loss of abandoned fishponds would account for about 0.1%.
9.6.2.7 The conditions of these abandoned fishponds are not suitable for short-term
resumption of fisheries activities given the physical constraints such as
inaccessibility, deterioration of pond bund, etc., and therefore not anticipated to
support significant fisheries production. Furthermore, considering the small loss of
abandoned fishponds does not account for a significant proportion of the total
fishponds area in Hong Kong and no evidence of commercial aquaculture activities
was observed in these abandoned fishponds during recent observation, the impact
on fisheries resources and fisheries production is considered negligible.
Loss of Watercourses for Aquaculture Activities
9.6.2.8 Under the Project, some of the watercourses would be temporarily affected during
the construction phase. However, except the small areas of pile cap areas (and

near NTMWTW. Moreover, the major water source for fishponds within the

9.6.3.2 9.6.3.3 Uncontrolled site run-off, sediment and chemical waste generated from construction
activities could potentially cause water quality impacts, including parameters such
as pH value, dissolved oxygen (DO) and salinity, to the adjacent watercourses and
water bodies. Moreover, the use and storage of chemicals (e.g. engine oil and
lubricants) during construction phase, may affect water quality if spillage occurs and
enters the adjacent water bodies and watercourses. Groundwater pollution may
also arise from improper handling and storage of chemicals within the works sites,
where groundwater infiltrates. Without mitigation measure, these potential water
quality impacts may result in potentially low to moderate impacts on the active and
inactive fishponds in the vicinity of the Project Boundary.
The examples of relevant water quality control measures and the details of these
mitigation measures are detailed in Section 5. Given the major water source for
fishponds within the Assessment Area would be from direct rainfall, with proper
implementation of the proposed mitigation measures, adverse impacts on water
quality are not anticipated. As a result, no adverse impacts on aquaculture activities
and fisheries production due to potential water quality deterioration is expected
during the construction phase.

9.6.3.4 9.6.3.5 9.6.3.6 9.6.3.7 Underground tunnelling works for tunnel section of the Project may potentially led
to groundwater drawdown and affect the fishponds in the vicinity. Nonetheless, the
tunnel sections of the Project would be in Ngau Tam Shan and to the east of
Hadden Hill, away from existing fishponds (Figures 9.4 to 9.6 and Figure 9.8).
Besides, direct rainfall has been the major water source for fishponds within the
Assessment Area. Thus, no adverse impacts on cultured fish due to potential water
table drawdown is anticipated during the construction phase.
Potential Vibration Impact
Potential vibration impact may arise from the tunnelling works of the Project.
Considering the underground works would be carried out in general at least 10 m
below the local ground level and the tunnel sections of the Project would be in Ngau
Tam Shan and to the east of Hadden Hill, i.e. away from the existing fishponds
(Figures 9.4 to 9.6 and Figure 9.8), potential vibration impact to fishponds is not
anticipated.
Bund Stability
Construction activities that occur adjacent or in close vicinity to the fishponds
located to the west of NTMWTW and near Ki Lun Tsuen area may affect the integrity
of the pond bunds, potentially resulting in instability of the pond structure, or water
seepage.
In the absence of mitigation measures, this indirect impact could inhibit pond usage
and result in potentially low to moderate impact on the retained active fishponds to
the west of NTMWTW and near Ki Lun Tsuen area. With appropriate mitigation
measures implemented to ensure the stability of the pond bund during construction
phase (e.g. sheet pile wall and associated grouting, further described in Section
9.8.2.2), adverse impacts on aquaculture activities are not anticipated.

proposed wetland compensation area as an ecological enhancement measure of
the overall NMH Project with expected benefits such as consolidating small and
fragmented ponds into larger wetland with enhanced connectivity and physical
modification of pond structures and pond bunds to allow more gently sloping banks
for wildlife usage etc. Full-scale implementation of the wetland compensation could
only proceed upon completion of permanent works and removal of temporary
works. After the establishment period, the proposed wetland compensation site will
be handed over to AFCD for habitat management, subject to prior written consent
of AFCD and sufficient recurrent cost allocated to AFCD. The feasibility to include
aquaculture activities in the proposed wetland compensation site would be explored
after the establishment period of the proposed wetland compensation site.

9.7.1.1 Cumulative impact may arise from the construction and operation of the Project,
due to interaction with other developments in the area. The list of concurrent

impose cumulative impact on aquaculture activities and production include the
Northern Metropolis Highway – Kwu Tung Section, Northern Metropolis Highway –
Tin Shui Wai Section, Development at NTM Area, Northern Link (NOL) Main Line,
NTMWTW Extension and STLMC DN.
9.7.1.2 Given the assessment of Northern Metropolis Highway – Kwu Tung Section and
Tin Shui Wai Section are still undergoing, relevant cumulative impact will be
assessed in subsequent EIA reports. In terms of the loss of fishponds under the
other concurrent projects within the Assessment Area, the loss under NOL Main
Line would be short-term loss and would be released upon the completion of
construction, while no direct loss of active fishponds is expected under NTMWTW
Extension (MTRCL, 2023; WSD, 2024). On the other hand, fishponds loss under

measures was proposed to enhance the fisheries resources (e.g. fisheries activities
and production, culture area and aquaculture potential etc.) of the proposed Sam
Po Shue Wetland Conservation Park with a view to compensate for the loss of
fishponds arising from the development of the San Tin Technopole (CEDD, 2024).
For Development at NTM area, the area of fishponds involved is considered as

9.8.2.1 In order to minimise the potential indirect fisheries impacts due to deterioration of
water quality, including parameters such as pH value, dissolved oxygen (DO) and
salinity, on the adjacent fishponds, mitigation measures and good site practices
would be implemented during the construction phase, details refer to Section 5.
Examples of guidelines for control of construction site run-off and construction-
related activities, as well as other good site practices, are described below. With
proper implementation of the proposed mitigation measures, adverse impacts on
water quality are not anticipated.
Control of Construction Site Run-off
• Implementation of Best Management Practices, following the guidelines for
handling and disposal of construction site discharges detailed in ProPECC PN
2/24 Construction Site Drainage and ETWB TC (Works) No. 5/2005 Protection
of Natural Streams / Rivers from Adverse Impacts Arising from Construction
Works;
• Controlling surface run-off from construction site via adequately designed
channels, earth bunds or sandbag barriers, and directing the run-off to sand /
silt removal facilities such as sand traps, silt traps and sedimentation basins
before discharging to storm drains;
• Minimising soil excavation in wet season (April to September) as far as
practicable, and proper covering of temporarily exposed slope surfaces, while
intercepting channels should be provided along the crest / edge of excavation;
and
• Proper covering of open stockpiles of construction materials during rainstorms
(e.g. with tarpaulin or similar fabric).
Control of Construction-related Activities
• All vehicles and plants should be cleaned before they leave the construction
site to minimise the deposition of earth, mud and debris in surrounding areas;
• Acidic wastewater generated from acid cleaning, etching, pickling and similar
activities should be neutralised to within the pH range of 6 to 10 before
discharging into foul sewers. If there is no public foul sewer in the vicinity, the
neutralised wastewater should be transported off site for disposal into foul
sewers or treated to a standard acceptable to storm drains and the receiving
waters; and
• The Waste Disposal Ordinance (Cap. 354) and its subsidiary regulations in
particular the Waste Disposal (Chemical Waste) (General) Regulation, should
be observed and complied with for control of chemical wastes. The Contractor
is also recommended to develop management procedures for chemicals used
and prepare an emergency spillage handling procedure to deal with chemical
spillage in case of accidents.
Maintaining Bund Stability
9.8.2.2 During the construction stage, retained active fishponds to the west of NTMWTW
and near Ki Lun Tsuen area should be isolated and disconnected from any existing
watercourses in order to minimise the potential water quality impact to the adjacent
water bodies. A layer of shoring or sheet pile wall should be erected along the
retained fishponds in order to maintain bund stability, where appropriate. In
